summary:
A wide-ranging conversation about always-on AI agents and how they change daily work, developer workflows and infrastructure bottlenecks. Kai Hendry and Vincent De Smet trade practical notes on Orca, Claude Code, Codex and Hermes, compare model behaviour, and explain how agent automation reshapes code review, pull requests and CI. They also discuss Omarchy and open-source politics, hardware and hosting costs, access to frontier models, and the engineering judgement needed to maintain agent-produced code.

[slide:1]
### [00:00] Personal agent workflows and model mix

The hosts start with contrasting approaches to switching off: Vincent tries to keep weekends free of work, while Kai uses agents throughout the day. Kai describes using Orca from his phone and another laptop, with OpenAI’s Astra 6 helping improve his existing projects. They discuss the practical trade-offs of always-on machines, subscriptions and API keys, and the value of using more than one model ecosystem. Remote access makes it easier to keep work moving, but also harder to establish boundaries.

[slide:2]
### [06:23] Stacked PRs and agentic code review

Vincent demonstrates stacked pull requests: dependent changes are organised into a sequence that reviewers can examine and merge in order. He has added support to Hermes so each PR is reviewed against the appropriate point in the stack. They compare this with asking Opus to split work into smaller commits, debating whether the commit or the PR is the useful unit of review. Kai worries that several stacked PRs could multiply the already lengthy descriptions generated by AI. The discussion moves on to remote review, Git tools and out-of-hours notifications.

[slide:3]
### [17:09] Omarchy, Linux on laptops and community politics

A long segment covers Omarchy, the DHH-led Arch Linux setup, as a practical route to a usable Linux desktop. Technical praise for installation and defaults sits alongside frustration with Mac hardware costs and macOS behaviour. The hosts also debate the political arguments surrounding open-source maintainers and donor-backed foundations, asking how much a founder’s views should influence a decision to use their software.

[slide:4]
### [30:12] Hardware, tokens and hosting trade-offs

Kai’s desire for computing independence runs into his reliance on frontier models and commercial devices. Vincent describes an expensive demonstration PC at a computer shop, prompting a comparison of local GPU inference with hosted models. Owning capable hardware is only part of the cost; operating it and getting useful performance also matter. From [36:15], they discuss model subscriptions, hosted agents and the barriers facing people who cannot afford expensive tools or easily access the required accounts and payment methods.

[slide:5]
### [40:40] Human accountability and the AI engineer role

Vincent expects employees to have several persistent agents acting on their behalf. The hosts agree that an agent may have its own bot identity, but a named human must remain responsible for its actions. From [44:40], they discuss teaching engineering and the importance of owning a product, understanding its architecture and operating what you build. Stories about refactoring fragile AI-generated systems lead them to argue that engineering judgement and operational experience remain valuable.

At [53:06], the conversation turns to specialist agent roles. Vincent prefers supplying the context and perspective needed for a task over maintaining fixed role profiles. He describes combining reviews from several angles and questions whether telling a model “you are an expert” discourages it from checking its assumptions.

[slide:6]
### [56:35] CI, attestations and the new bottlenecks

They revisit a proposal for verifiable attestations of tests already run by an agent, asking whether CI needs to repeat the same work. An article about growing CI workloads leads to a discussion of larger runners, sharding and the limits of adding capacity. The hosts want more technical detail from AI companies about verification, integrations and infrastructure, and compare those articles with older engineering write-ups, including the Kubernetes Failure Stories collection shown on screen.

From [1:07:48], Vincent makes the case for Backstage and MCP as a source of service ownership, dependencies and operational context for agents, while Kai questions the practical experience behind that recommendation. Spotify’s agent adoption raises the broader question of whether faster delivery improves the product. At [1:13:00], they explore collaborative comments on Claude and Kiro artifacts, including the friction of sending feedback back to an agent. They close with listener comments and the Agent Client Protocol.

A wide-ranging conversation about always‑on AI agents and how they change daily work, developer workflows and infrastructure bottlenecks. Speakers trade practical notes on using multiple agent platforms (Orca, Claude/Codex, cloud code), compare model behavior, and explain how agentic automation reshapes code review, PR organization and CI. The discussion also touches on desktop OS choices (the Omari/Arch debate), hardware and hosting costs, access inequality for AI tools, the emerging role of “AI engineers” who must clean up agent‑produced code, and persistent integration and CI bottlenecks at scale.

[slide:1]
## Personal agent workflows and model mix
Speakers start by describing personal setups: one avoids work over weekends while another uses agents continuously—Orca for organizing sessions and OpenAI’s Astra 6 for rapid creative/3D workflows—finding these tools surprisingly transformative for day‑to‑day productivity. They note practical tradeoffs (charging always‑online laptops, switching between cloud and local keys) and the value of running multiple models side‑by‑side to pick better outputs. *it's pretty much changed my life in the last like 10 days.*

[slide:2]
## Stacked PRs and agentic code review
They explain stacked PRs as a response to large AI‑generated PRs: instead of one huge PR, multiple PRs stack so dependent changes can be reviewed and merged in order, reducing rebases and letting reviewers focus on units of work. Opus and similar tools can slice commits, while agents like Hermas perform per‑PR reviews in a stack; this shifts reviewer workflows and raises questions about when and how humans vs agents approve changes.

[slide:3]
## Omari, Linux on laptops, and community politics
A long segment covers Omari (a DHH‑led Arch Linux installer/packaging effort), framed as a pragmatic gateway to Linux for teams fed up with Mac hardware costs and MacOS quirks. Conversation mixes technical praise (fast installs, usable defaults) with the social fallout around a founder’s politics and donor‑backed foundations, arguing people should weigh technical utility separately from political disagreement.

[slide:4]
## Hardware, tokens and hosting tradeoffs
They compare local high‑end machines versus cloud inference: a demo machine’s GPU can be ~30% of a high price tag and deliver tens of tokens/second per LLM, but owning and hosting such hardware is expensive and often impractical. The speakers accept some hypocrisy—advocating independence while relying on cloud services—and worry about access gaps for developers in regions without cheap model access.

[slide:5]
## AI‑produced code, technical debt and the AI engineer role
Several anecdotes show companies that cut engineering teams expecting agents to replace developers ended up with fragile, unarchitected systems. The panel predicts renewed demand for engineers who can perform architectural reviews, refactor AI‑generated “slop,” and design for operational costs—an emergent “AI engineer” competency combining product thinking and deep operational experience.

[slide:6]
## CI, attestations and the new bottlenecks
They dive into recent articles arguing CI has become the bottleneck as agentic workflows and review automation scale: agentic reviews can attest they ran tests, but practical systems still re‑run CI; teams shard jobs to buy time but encounter new complexity. The group critiques some vendor writeups as shallow, highlights agent context providers (Backstage, artifacts, MCP) as useful for agents, and stresses that integrations, verification/attestation and robust sandboxing remain hard engineering problems. *agentic reviews so now CI is the bottleneck*
